analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from forcing workers into arbitration to settle workplace disputes.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Millions of American workers sign agreements as a condition of hiring that force any dispute over pay, discrimination, or firing into private arbitration instead of court, where cases are heard alone, in secret, with no appeal. This bill would make those pre-dispute arbitration agreements unenforceable. Workers could still choose arbitration after a dispute arises, but only voluntarily, with a written explanation and a 45-day waiting period, and employers could not punish anyone who refuses. It would also void agreements that bar workers from joining class or collective actions and add protections against retaliation under labor law.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 60 million-plus American workers covered by forced arbitration clauses in their employment agreements — including hourly workers, gig workers treated as independent contractors, and domestic workers — who would regain the right to go to court, join class actions over wage theft or discrimination, and have disputes heard in public with the possibility of appeal.

how_it_helps.text: Invalidates any pre-dispute arbitration agreement requiring arbitration of a work dispute, so employers can no longer make signing away court access a condition of getting hired [S3].

Allows post-dispute arbitration only if it is truly voluntary: no coercion, plain-language written notice of the right to refuse, a 45-day waiting period with tolling of the statute of limitations, and written consent [S3].

Protects class and collective actions: voids agreements that forbid workers from bringing or joining joint, class, or collective claims, restoring the main tool for challenging small-dollar wage violations affecting many workers at once [S3].

Bars retaliation — with a private right of action, attorney's fees, and up to treble back pay under civil rights remedies — against workers who refuse to arbitrate, and covers independent contractors regardless of how the employer labels them [S3].
Amends the National Labor Relations Act to make it an unfair labor practice to enter into or enforce agreements that give up the right to pursue joint, class, or collective claims about work [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who rely on mandatory arbitration clauses — large retail, restaurant, gig, and staffing companies in particular — lose a system that keeps disputes private, heard one worker at a time, with limited appeal and low employer win rates in court-facing alternatives. The commercial arbitration industry loses a large, employer-driven volume of mandatory employment cases. Court systems would also handle more employment filings.

drawbacks.text: Court litigation is slower and more expensive than arbitration for an individual worker, so some single-victim disputes could take longer to resolve without arbitration as the default [S3].

The bill would substantially raise litigation exposure for employers across wage, discrimination, and termination claims, a cost that honest supporters acknowledge is the point: employers lose the shield of one-at-a-time, private, hard-to-appeal dispute resolution [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefits are large and well-documented: forced arbitration strips access to court, blocks class actions that make small claims viable, and keeps disputes secret. The costs fall almost entirely on employers and arbitration providers, plus a modest increase in court caseloads. Some workers with strong single claims might prefer arbitration's speed, but the bill preserves that option — it only requires it be chosen after a dispute, voluntarily.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on July 29, 2021, sat in the House Judiciary Committee and the Education and Labor Committee, was sent to a Judiciary subcommittee a year later, and never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler introduced the bill on July 29, 2021 with 36 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S3].
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and the House Education and Labor Committee on the day of introduction [S5].

On November 1, 2022 — over a year later, and about two months before the Congress ended — it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law; that was the last action of record [S5].
No committee markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever took place, and the bill died at the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that rely on mandatory arbitration clauses keep their ability to route workplace disputes into private arbitration, and the arbitration industry keeps that volume of business. Workers covered by forced arbitration agreements are no better off.

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Restoring Justice for Workers Act to ban forced arbitration in work disputes.

for.name: 39 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Rep. Bobby Scott (Chair, Education and Labor) and Rep. Hank Johnson (Chair, Judiciary Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law).

sides.party_line_note: All 40 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the House Republican leadership that controlled scheduling never brought the bill to a committee vote or the floor [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Large employers using mandatory arbitration (retail, restaurants, gig platforms, staffing firms)
industries.note: The bill would invalidate the pre-dispute clauses these companies use to keep workplace disputes out of court, heard one worker at a time, and block class actions. Their interest in keeping the status quo runs directly against workers' access to legal remedies.

Mandatory employment arbitration generates a large, employer-paid caseload; the bill keeps only voluntary post-dispute arbitration, shrinking the market. Its revenue depends on the practice the bill would ban.
Restored access to court and class actions would expand the market for attorneys representing workers, including through fee-shifting provisions in the bill.
